questions.stem: What keeps a moon in orbit around its planet?

options.text: the gravitational attraction of the planet
options.explanation: Gravity towards the larger body bends the moon's path into an orbit.
Moons are natural; no engines exist.
Orbits are gravitational, not magnetic.
The planet's pull is what curves the path.

questions.stem: In an orbit, the gravitational force on the smaller body points…

options.explanation: The dominant pull is from the orbited body.

options.text: towards the centre of the larger body
options.explanation: The attraction always aims at the larger body's centre.
Attraction pulls inward, never outward.
The force is not along the motion; that is why the path curves.

questions.stem: Which pairing of orbiter and orbited body is correct?

options.explanation: The larger body is orbited, not the orbiter.
Satellites orbit the Earth.
The Sun anchors the planetary orbits.
Moons orbit planets.

questions.stem: Artificial satellites stay in orbit around the Earth because of…

options.explanation: Air resistance would drag satellites down.
Speed alone cannot curve the path; force is required.
Solar wind does not hold satellites.
Gravity supplies the inward force the orbit needs.

questions.stem: Comets travel around…

options.text: the Sun, on stretched elliptical paths
options.explanation: Comets are Sun-orbiters with highly elliptical orbits.
Comets orbit the Sun, not the Earth.
Neither the body nor the shape is right.
The course-level answer is comets orbit the Sun.

questions.stem: State what causes orbital motion.
questions.modelAnswer: Orbital motion results from the gravitational force of attraction acting between the two bodies.

questions.stem: Name the force that keeps satellites in orbit around the Earth.
questions.modelAnswer: The Earth's gravitational pull keeps artificial satellites in orbit.

questions.stem: Explain why the gravitational force makes an orbiting body move in a circular path.
questions.modelAnswer: The pull always points towards the centre of the larger body, so the smaller body is constantly steered inward — a steady inward turn of its motion traces out a circular path.

questions.stem: Classify each orbit: our Moon, the planet Neptune, a weather satellite, and Halley's-type comet.
questions.modelAnswer: The Moon orbits a planet; Neptune orbits the Sun; the satellite orbits the Earth; the comet orbits the Sun on a highly elliptical path.

questions.stem: How do the orbits of the planets compare in direction and plane?

options.explanation: Retrograde motion is not the shared pattern.

options.text: they all travel the same direction around the Sun, in the same plane
options.explanation: Shared plane and direction are two of the planet similarities.

options.text: each planet picks its own plane and direction
options.explanation: Planets share plane and direction.
The directions are common, not random.

questions.stem: The further a planet sits from the Sun, the…

options.explanation: Distant planets take longer.
All planetary orbits are slightly elliptical already.

options.text: slower it travels and the longer its orbit takes
options.explanation: Distance up, speed down, period up.
Near planets are the fast ones.

questions.stem: A moon orbits its planet in…

options.text: a highly elliptical path like a comet
options.explanation: That is comet behaviour.

options.text: a straight line past the planet
options.explanation: A straight line is not an orbit.

options.text: an orbit around the Sun instead
options.explanation: Moons orbit planets.
Moons follow circular orbits around their planets.

questions.stem: Bringing a moon closer to its planet makes its orbit…

options.explanation: Closer moons race round in less time.
That is what distance does, not closeness.
Speed depends on distance.
Orbits do not stand upright like that.

questions.stem: Which statement about planetary orbital radii is right?

options.explanation: Orbital radii stay effectively fixed.

options.text: planets orbit at different distances from the Sun
options.explanation: Radii differ — that is one of the listed differences.

options.text: all planets share the same orbital radius
options.explanation: Radii differ between planets.

options.text: orbital radius has no effect on speed
options.explanation: Radius sets speed: distant planets are slower.

questions.stem: State the shared features of the planets' orbits.
questions.modelAnswer: Their orbits are slightly elliptical with the Sun near the centre, they share one plane, and they travel the same direction.

questions.stem: State how a moon's orbit changes as it sits closer to its planet.
questions.modelAnswer: The closer moon completes each orbit in less time and at greater speed.

questions.stem: Explain why distant planets take longer to orbit the Sun.
questions.modelAnswer: The further a planet sits from the Sun, the slower it travels along its orbit, and with a longer path to cover at lower speed each circuit takes more time.

questions.stem: Two planets, X near the Sun and Y far out. Compare their orbital speeds and periods.
questions.modelAnswer: Planet X, nearer the Sun, travels faster and completes each orbit sooner; planet Y travels more slowly and takes longer for each circuit.

questions.stem: The shape of a comet's orbit is…

options.explanation: No orbit is square.
Comet orbits differ sharply from planetary ones.
Stretched ellipses and hyperbolas are comet territory.
Comet orbits are strongly stretched.

questions.stem: As a comet approaches the Sun, its speed…

options.explanation: Comet speed changes with distance.
That happens on the outward leg.

options.text: drops to zero at closest approach
options.explanation: Closest approach is the fastest point.
Approach means speed-up; recession means slow-down.

questions.stem: As a comet moves away from the Sun, its speed…

options.explanation: Distance gained is speed lost.
The speed-up belongs to the approach.
Speed varies along the orbit.
Speed has nothing to do with shape here.

questions.stem: Comet orbits compared with planetary orbits…

options.text: never pass close to the Sun
options.explanation: Close approaches are the hallmark of comet orbits.

options.text: need not share the planets' plane and may run the opposite direction
options.explanation: Inclination and direction are not fixed for comets.

options.text: always lie in the planets' plane
options.explanation: Comets are not confined to that plane.

options.text: always run the same direction as planets
options.explanation: Some comets run counter to the planets.

questions.stem: Why does a comet's speed change significantly along its orbit?

options.text: because the Sun's gravity vanishes far away
options.explanation: Gravity weakens with distance but never vanishes.
Collisions are not part of the orbital story.

options.text: its distance from the Sun changes dramatically on the stretched orbit
options.explanation: Large distance swings drive large speed swings.
Comets have no engines.

questions.stem: Describe the shape of a comet's orbit.
questions.modelAnswer: A comet's orbit is highly elliptical — very stretched — or hyperbolic.

questions.stem: State how a comet's speed changes during one orbit.
questions.modelAnswer: The comet speeds up as it approaches the Sun and slows down as it moves away.

questions.stem: Explain why comet orbits differ so much from planetary orbits.
questions.modelAnswer: Comets follow highly elliptical or hyperbolic paths rather than the planets' near-circular, single-plane circles, so their distance from the Sun — and hence their speed — swings enormously, and their planes and directions need not match the planets'.

questions.stem: A comet is observed slowing down over successive nights. State where it is in its orbit relative to the Sun.
questions.modelAnswer: The comet is moving away from the Sun on the outward leg of its orbit, where its speed decreases.
